hints: Count the number of L ligands bonded to J in each diagram to get the coordination number, then recall which regular 3D arrangement spreads that many bonds furthest apart.
Remember the standard ideal angles for the four common arrangements: four bonds in 3D, four bonds in one plane, six bonds in 3D, and two bonds in a line.
walkthrough:
Read the diagrams as coordination numbers**
Think of J in the centre and L at the ends of the sticks. P has 4 L groups arranged in 3D with wedge and dashed bonds. Q has 4 L groups all drawn in one flat cross. R has 6 L groups in 3D. S has only 2 L groups in a straight line. So the coordination numbers are 4, 4, 6 and 2.

Match each count to its ideal geometry**
Four bonds can spread out in two very different ways. P uses the 3D way to keep all four as far apart as possible, giving the tetrahedral angle of $109.5^\circ$. Q forces all four into one plane, giving $90^\circ$ between neighbours and $180^\circ$ across the centre. Six bonds gives the octahedral arrangement with $90^\circ$ between neighbours and $180^\circ$ opposite. Two bonds can only point opposite each other to avoid each other, giving $180^\circ$ for S.

Final answer: P $109.5^\circ$ (accept $109^\circ$); Q $90^\circ$ (adjacent) or $180^\circ$ (opposite);
R $90^\circ$ (adjacent) or $180^\circ$ (opposite); S $180^\circ$.

hints: Use the wedge, dashed and ordinary lines to decide if the four-coordinate complexes are truly 3D or flat in one plane.
Recall the specific Cambridge names for 4-coordinate 3D, 4-coordinate planar, 6-coordinate and 2-coordinate complexes.
walkthrough:
Separate the two types of 4-coordinate**
This is the classic trap. Both P and Q have formula $\text{JL}_{4}$ but they look different. P shows solid wedge and dashed bonds, which is the drawing convention for coming out of and going behind the plane. That means 3D tetrahedral. Q is drawn as a simple flat cross with all $\text{L-J-L}$ in the same plane, which is square planar.

Name R and S directly**
R has six monodentate L ligands, three mutually perpendicular axes with J at the centre. That is the definition of octahedral. S has only two ligands, $\text{L-J-L}$ in a straight line. That is linear. No other names are accepted for these coordination numbers with monodentate ligands.

Final answer: P tetrahedral; Q square planar;
R octahedral; S linear.

hints: Ask for each new complex whether the two new ligands X and Y can be placed next to each other in one isomer and opposite each other in a different isomer.
walkthrough:
Test what cis and trans really needs**
Picture replacing two L by X and Y. For geometrical isomerism you need a structure where X and Y can be $90^\circ$ apart in one complex (cis) and $180^\circ$ apart in another (trans). That needs $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ positions to exist in the parent shape.

Apply to P, Q, R and S**
In tetrahedral P every position is $109.5^\circ$ from every other position, so there is no opposite position and no cis versus trans pair. In linear S the product is simply $\text{X-J-Y}$ with only $180^\circ$, so only one form. In square planar Q, X and Y can be adjacent ($90^\circ$, cis) or opposite ($180^\circ$, trans). In octahedral R the same is true, X and Y can be $90^\circ$ apart or $180^\circ$ apart. So only Q and R show geometrical isomerism.

hints: Recall that optical isomerism needs a complex with no mirror plane or centre of symmetry, most simply four different groups in a tetrahedral arrangement or a suitable unsymmetrical octahedral arrangement.
walkthrough:
Build the new formulas in your head**
Replacing three L by three different ligands X, Y and Z gives: from tetrahedral P, $\text{J(L)(X)(Y)(Z)}$ with four all different groups; from square planar Q, $\text{J(L)(X)(Y)(Z)}$ flat in one plane; from octahedral R, $\text{J(L)}_{3}\text{(X)(Y)(Z)}$ with six ligands including three different new ones.

Decide which can be chiral**
The tetrahedral product from P is just like a chiral carbon with four different groups. Its mirror image cannot be superimposed, so it exists as a pair of enantiomers. Square planar complexes are always flat and so always have a mirror plane through the molecular plane, they can never be chiral, so Q is out. An octahedral complex with three different monodentate replacements can arrange X, Y and Z so that the mirror image is non-superimposable, giving non-superimposable mirror images. So P and R show optical isomerism.
